implementation_notes: Java's modern default: the DTO is a record, which replaces the classic mutable JavaBean with a one-line immutable declaration (fields, canonical constructor, accessors, equals/hashCode/toString), while a JSON library performs the serialization that Java itself only offers through the discouraged java.io.Serializable machinery - Jackson recognises record components as properties from 2.12 on, without annotations. Component names are the JSON keys, so casing is configured once via a naming strategy. Keep the JavaBean form only when a framework demands a no-argument constructor or settable properties.
pitfalls: Record accessors are named id(), not getId(), and are final: naming strategies that rely on getX prefixes do not apply, and transport conveniences must live in a compact constructor or companion helpers.

java.io.Serializable is not a wire format: it couples both sides to the same class version, has a long history of deserialization gadget attacks and is restricted in modern JDKs - use JSON, CBOR or protobuf.
Nullability is not expressed: a null field is silently null unless the compact constructor validates, so half-built DTOs are possible.

variants.name: Classic JavaBean + Jackson
variants.implementation_notes: The classic PoEAA-era realization: a mutable class with a public no-argument constructor, private fields and getter/setter pairs, serialized by Jackson, JSON-B or the platform's Serializable machinery. It remains necessary where a framework contract requires instantiate-then-populate (JPA entities, some XML and bean-mapping frameworks) or where bean-style introspection with getX/isX naming is what the tooling expects. Otherwise the record form removes both the boilerplate and the mutability.
pitfalls: Setters allow any holder to rewrite the payload and validation has no single home, so invariants cannot be enforced.
Bean introspection depends on naming conventions: renaming getCustomer without updating the serializer silently changes the wire field.
